issues.description: Method signature mismatch for SealSaloon.acceptSupplyDelivery: The problem statement (UML and textual description) declares acceptSupplyDelivery with four parameters (supplier name, ingredient name, price, quantity), but the template/solution code and example calls use a three-parameter signature acceptSupplyDelivery(String ingredientName, int price, int quantity). This inconsistency leaves students unsure which signature to implement and which calls/examples are correct.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the acceptSupplyDelivery signature consistent across the problem statement, UML, template examples, and solution. Either: (A) Update the UML and textual description to declare acceptSupplyDelivery(String ingredientName, int price, int quantity) and adjust the UML/method documentation to remove the supplier parameter; or (B) update the template and solution to implement acceptSupplyDelivery(String supplierName, String ingredientName, int price, int quantity) and update all example calls (Main) and tests accordingly. Ensure the chosen signature is used consistently in the UML, problem text, example code, and tests.

issues.description: Conflicting instructions about SealSaloon.stock initialization and scope: The problem statement instructs that the SealSaloon attributes (orders and final Stock stock) "should be initialized ... in the constructor of SealSaloon" while elsewhere the text explicitly requires the stock attribute to be static (shared across all instances). The solution declares stock as a static final field and initializes it at its declaration. These two instructions (initialize in instance constructor vs. static/shared attribute) contradict each other and will confuse students about where and how to declare/initialize stock.
issues.suggestedFix: Clarify the intended scope and initialization strategy for the stock attribute. Either: (A) If stock is intended to be shared across all SealSaloon instances, state that stock should be declared static (for example: private static final Stock stock = new Stock();) and instruct students to initialize it at declaration or in a static initializer (not in the instance constructor); or (B) if stock should be an instance-level final field, remove the requirement that it be static and instruct students to initialize it in the no-argument constructor. Update the problem text, UML, and any examples to reflect the chosen design.
